title: Multi-level CMS Reproduction (Nested Learning Trend)
formal_question: Can a small-scale (135M backbone, 5.3M memory) continual memory system reproduce the hierarchical timescale performance trend reported in the Nested Learning paper (2512.24695v1)?
expected_comparison: Controlled comparison of 1-level (B4) vs 2-level (A2) vs 3-level (B5/P1) memory under identical context and retrieval conditions.

audit_findings.claim_in_round2_report: P2 achieves 0.183 F1 on QASPER (+47.6% over B1: 0.124), demonstrating superior hierarchical compression.
audit_findings.scientific_flaw: Conflation of retrieval effect with hierarchical memory effect. P2 is a hybrid system combining SA-CMS memory with BM25 retrieval, whereas B1 is an un-retrieved full-context prompt. The +47.6% improvement is primarily driven by BM25 evidence selection, NOT isolated hierarchical timescale dynamics.
audit_findings.trend_reproduction_analysis: On QASPER and LongHealth under context-evicted conditions, 1-level B4 actually scored higher than 3-level B5 and P1. The monotonic improvement with memory levels (1-lvl < 2-lvl < 3-lvl) from the Nested Learning paper is ONLY observed in MK-NIAH target token probability (P1 0.1318 > B4 0.0479 > B5 0.0349), but does not translate into answer classification accuracy (0% across all memory models at 200 training samples).
audit_findings.required_remedy: Re-label RQ1 claim. State honestly: At the 135M student scale with 200 training samples, hierarchical memory increases target token probability on key retrieval but does not reproduce full end-to-end task accuracy gains without hybrid non-parametric retrieval.
